Abstract—This study identifies risk factors for atrial 
fibrillation (AF) in 473 Korean diagnosed with AF. In a 
survival analysis of demographic characteristics such as age, 
sex, and BMI, and the presence of hypertension, stroke, and 
coronary artery disease diagnosis before AF diagnosis, 
hypertension and stroke were identified as risk factors for AF, 
with hazard ratios of 1.480 and 1.542, respectively. 
Clinical Relevance—Exploring risk factors may be used to 
predict the development of AF or to manage its prognosis. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Several risk factors have been implicated in the 
pathogenesis of AF, including obesity, sleep apnea, excessive 
alcohol consumption, vigorous exercise, hypertension (HTN), 
and systemic inflammation. Additionally, comorbidities such 
as coronary artery disease (CAD) and stroke (STK) may 
predispose individuals to AF [1]. However, whether these 
factors are conclusive indicators of atrial fibrillation risk 
remains controversial. The aim of this study is to reaffirm 
effects of demographic characteristics and associated diseases 
as risk factors for AF. We collect diagnostic and 
demographic information on atrial fibrillation and use 
survival analysis to explore risk factors for AF. 
II. METHODS 
This study was conducted retrospectively using data from 
patients who visited Asan Medical Center (Seoul, South 
Korea) from January 2013 to October 2023. We collected 
anonymized datasets that included variables such as patient 
ID, sex, age, body mass index (BMI), and disease conditions 
of HTN, AF, STK and CAD. The data screening process 
involved several stages: (1) identification of patients 
diagnosed with AF, STK, HTN, or CAD; (2) exclusion of 
patients without an AF diagnosis; (3) removal of patients

whose initial diagnosis within the study timeframe was AF; 
(4) acquisition of BMI values recorded on the AF diagnosis 
date; (5) compilation of pre-AF diagnosis comorbidities; (6) 
calculation of the interval in months between the last visit 
prior to AF diagnosis and the initial AF diagnosis, excluding 
those diagnosed with AF within one month of another disease 
diagnosis; and (7) elimination of records with missing data. 
Applying these criteria resulted in a cohort of 473 patients 
from a pool of 5,180 initial AF patients, details of which are 
shown in Table I. We employed the Cox-Proportional-
Hazards (CPH) model to evaluate the influence of various 
factors on the AF, deriving hazard ratios and 95% confidence 
intervals for each. The categorization of age and BMI within 
the CPH model adhered to the World Health Organization's 
criteria for aging (≥60 years) and overweight (≥25 kg/m2), 
respectively. All statistical computations, including data 
preprocessing and analysis, were conducted using Python 
(version 3.11.4), with the 'lifelines' package facilitating the 
construction of the CPH model. 
III. RESULTS 
Table II shows the prevalence of each evaluated factor 
among AF patients, alongside the corresponding hazard ratios 
ascertained through the CPH model. The data indicates a 
predominance of older age in the AF cohort, with 86. 1% 
being aged ≥60 years. Additionally, males constituted 60.0% 
of AF patients, and 63.6% of AF patients were previously 
diagnosed with HTN. According to the hazard ratio analysis, 
HTN (HR=1.480) and STK (HR=1.542) appear to be 
significant predictors of AF. Conversely, older age, male 
gender, being overweight, and the presence of CAD did not 
exhibit a statistically significant risk association with the 
onset of AF. 
IV. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION 
The study reaffirmed that HTN and STK are risk factors 
for AF in Koreans. One limitation is that a significant amount 
of data was not included in the analysis because we removed 
missing values where they existed without estimating or 
interpolating. We expect to apply improved missing value 
processing strategies to obtain more reliable results.
